blocks.text: How fast should standing water be removed from a Midvale home?

segments.t: Within the first few hours. After 24 to 48 hours, drywall, carpet pad and subfloors absorb the water and mold risk rises, even in Utah's dry air.

Water does not sit still. It runs to the lowest point, slides under baseboards, and soaks into the pad beneath carpet before it shows on top. Drywall acts like a sponge and can wick water well above the visible waterline within a day. Particleboard subfloors and cabinet bases swell and lose strength. Clean water from a supply line also changes over time: after about 48 hours, bacteria growth turns it into gray water, which means more materials have to come out instead of being dried in place. That is why the clock matters more than anything else on an extraction job.

blocks.text: Why does water come up through a Midvale basement floor with no leak?

segments.t: Snowmelt and heavy watering saturate Midvale's clay soil and raise groundwater near the Jordan River, and that pressure pushes water up through slab cracks and wall joints.

blocks.text: Does Midvale's hard water make water heaters fail sooner?

segments.t: Yes. Hard water leaves scale in the tank bottom, which overheats the steel and wears the anode rod, so tanks in basement utility rooms can leak or fail suddenly.

Midvale's drinking water comes from city wells and from the Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District, and like most Salt Lake Valley water it carries a lot of dissolved calcium and magnesium. When that water is heated, the minerals settle at the bottom of the tank as a layer of scale. The burner or element has to work through that layer, the steel runs hotter, and the anode rod that protects the tank from rust gets used up faster. The same scale builds up inside valves, washer inlet screens, dishwasher lines and ice-maker fittings. Over years, small leaks turn into sudden ones.

blocks.text: Why is my swamp cooler leaking through the ceiling in Midvale?

blocks.text: Can mold grow in Midvale homes when Utah air is so dry?

segments.t: Yes. Utah's outdoor air is dry, but a wet wall cavity or finished basement stays humid inside, and mold can start on wet drywall within 24 to 48 hours.

The dry air outside doesn't reach the inside of a wet wall. When water soaks drywall, insulation, carpet pad or wood, the space right around that material stays damp for days or weeks, even if the room feels dry. Mold spores are already present in every home. All they need is moisture, something to eat, like the paper on drywall or the dust in carpet, and time. Finished basements, wall cavities behind leaking pipes, attics under swamp coolers and crawl spaces give them all three. That's why most mold calls in Midvale follow a leak that was dried too slowly, or never found.

blocks.text: How do you find a hidden water leak in a Midvale home without opening walls?

segments.t: Thermal imaging shows cool, wet areas behind drywall, and moisture meters confirm them, so the leak path is traced with few or no holes before repairs start.

Wet materials show up cooler than dry ones on a thermal camera because evaporation pulls heat from them. That creates a pattern on the screen: a cool band down a wall, a spreading patch on a ceiling, a line along the floor. Thermal imaging doesn't see water directly, so every cool spot is checked with moisture meters. Pinless meters scan surfaces quickly; pin meters confirm how wet a material is at a specific point. Together they map exactly where water has traveled, which tells us, the plumber and your insurer where the source is and how far the damage goes.

Turn off every faucet, appliance, irrigation system and the water softener regeneration.
Find the water meter, usually in a box near the street.
Note the reading or watch the small leak indicator dial.
Wait about 30 minutes without using any water.
Check again. If the reading changed or the indicator moved, water is leaking somewhere.
This tells you a leak exists. Finding where it is takes the tools below.

pages.metaTitle: How to Keep Pipes From Freezing in Midvale | What to Do If One Bursts
pages.metaDescription: Where Midvale pipes freeze, how to thaw them safely, and the first steps after a burst. Call (385) 337-3560 for 24/7 help.
pages.h1: How to Keep Pipes From Freezing in Midvale, and What to Do If One Bursts
pages.intro: To keep pipes from freezing in Midvale, insulate pipes in crawl spaces, garages and outside walls, disconnect garden hoses before the first hard freeze, keep the heat steady at night, and let a faucet drip during the coldest spells. If a pipe bursts, shut off the main valve first, then deal with the water.

blocks.text: At what temperature do pipes freeze in Midvale homes?

segments.t: Exposed pipes can freeze once outdoor temperatures stay below about 20°F for several hours, especially in crawl spaces, garages and outside walls.

The number on the thermometer is only part of it. What matters is how cold the pipe itself gets and for how long. A pipe in a heated room rarely freezes. A pipe in an uninsulated rim joist, a garage wall or a crawl space near a vent can freeze on a night that doesn't feel especially cold, because wind and cold air reach it directly. In the Salt Lake Valley, cold air can also settle on the valley floor for days at a time during winter inversions, so homes in Midvale can sit through long stretches of below-freezing nights. The longer the cold lasts, the more pipes are at risk.

blocks.text: Where Midvale Pipes Freeze First

segments.t: Every home is different, but these are the spots that freeze most often in Midvale:
Rim joists:
the band of framing where the floor sits on the foundation. Pipes running along it in basements get cold air from outside.
Cantilevered floors:
in many 1960s to 1980s split-levels around Hillcrest and Union Park, part of the floor hangs past the wall below, with pipes inside.
Garage walls and ceilings:
supply lines running through an unheated garage to a kitchen or bathroom.
Crawl spaces:
common in older homes near Historic Main Street and Center Street, often with old galvanized lines.
Outside walls:
kitchen sinks and bathrooms on exterior walls, especially with cabinets that block warm air.
Hose bibs:
outside faucets, especially with a hose still attached.
Swamp cooler water lines:
small lines running to rooftop coolers that weren't shut off for winter.
If you know where your pipes run, you know where to focus.

blocks.text: Why the Hose Bib Matters So Much

segments.t: Many outside faucets are designed so the shut-off sits inside the wall where it stays warm. But when a hose is left connected, water stays trapped in the faucet body. That water freezes, splits the pipe inside the wall, and you won't see anything until spring, when you turn the faucet on and water runs into the wall or basement instead of out the spout. Disconnecting hoses in fall is one of the easiest ways to prevent a hidden burst.

blocks.text: How to Keep Pipes From Freezing: A Midvale Checklist

segments.t: Before the first hard freeze (usually October):
Disconnect and drain garden hoses.
Shut off and drain any outside faucets that have separate inside valves.
Shut off and drain the swamp cooler water line.
Drain and blow out sprinkler systems.
Insulate exposed pipes in crawl spaces, garages and along rim joists.
Seal gaps where cold air gets in near pipes, especially around sill plates and pipe penetrations.
Close crawl space vents.
Find your main shut-off valve and make sure it turns.
During cold spells:
Keep the thermostat steady day and night, at least in the mid-60s.
Open cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls.
Let a faucet on an outside wall drip slowly overnight.
Keep the garage door closed if pipes run through the garage.
If you travel, leave the heat on and ask someone to check the house.

blocks.text: Signs a Pipe Is Already Frozen

segments.t: Little or no water comes out of a faucet when you turn it on.
Frost on a visible pipe.
A faucet works on one side of the house but not the other.
A strange smell from a drain, as air can't move through the line.
If you see these, assume the pipe may already be split, even if nothing is leaking yet. The leak usually starts when it thaws.

blocks.text: How to Thaw a Frozen Pipe Safely

segments.t: Shut off the main water valve first
if you suspect a split, so thawing doesn't start a flood.
Open the faucet
the pipe feeds, so water and steam can escape as it thaws.
Warm the pipe gently
with a hair dryer, a heating pad, or a space heater kept at a safe distance. Start nearest the faucet and work back.
Never use an open flame
like a torch or lighter. It can damage the pipe and start a fire inside the wall.
Check for leaks
as water starts moving again. If water appears in a wall, ceiling or floor, shut the main off again.
Call a plumber
if you can't reach or thaw the pipe, or if it's inside a wall.

blocks.text: What to Do in the First 15 Minutes After a Burst

segments.t: If a pipe bursts, speed matters more than anything else.
Shut off the main water valve.
In most Midvale homes it's in the basement or utility room where the water line enters, often near the water heater.
Turn off power
to wet rooms at the breaker, if you can reach it without standing in water.
Open a faucet
on the lowest floor to drain pressure from the lines.
Move belongings
out of the water: rugs, electronics, furniture, boxes.
Take photos and video
of the water, the damage and the broken pipe.
Call a plumber
to repair the pipe.
Call a water damage crew
at (385) 337-3560 to remove the water and dry the structure. Burst Pipe Water Damage (/burst-pipe-water-damage/)

blocks.text: Why Burst Pipe Damage Spreads Inside Walls

segments.t: A split pipe inside a wall doesn't just leak onto the floor. Water runs down the inside of the wall cavity, soaks the insulation, pools on the bottom plate and spreads under flooring into the next room. The drywall face may look dry while the inside stays wet. That's why burst pipes need more than a mop and a fan: moisture meters and thermal imaging show how far the water went, and drying has to reach inside the wall cavity. Emergency Water Extraction (/emergency-water-extraction/)

blocks.text: Does Insurance Cover Frozen Pipes in Utah?

segments.t: Most Utah homeowners policies cover sudden water damage from a pipe that froze and split. They usually don't cover the repair of the pipe itself, damage from a slow leak that went on for a long time, or damage in a home that wasn't kept heated. Policies vary, so check yours. Photos, dates and records of when the leak was found help your claim either way.

blocks.text: Frozen Pipes in Midvale Rentals and Condos

segments.t: More than half of Midvale homes are rented, and many sit in multi-unit buildings. Vacant units between tenants and units with the heat turned down for travel are the most likely to freeze. A burst in one unit can damage the units below and beside it. Landlords and property managers should keep heat on in empty units and check them during cold spells. Tenants should tell their manager right away if water pressure drops during a freeze. Condo & Apartment Water Damage (/condo-apartment-water-damage/)

blocks.text: Which Midvale Homes Are Most at Risk

rows: Older bungalows near Historic Main Street
Insulate crawl space pipes and close vents in winter
1960s to 1980s split-levels in Hillcrest and Union Park
Pipes in cantilevered floors and rim joists
Keep the garage door closed in cold snaps
Townhomes and condos in Bingham Junction and Jordan Bluffs
Lines near exterior walls, sprinkler lines in cold spaces
Keep units heated, even when empty
Any home with an outside faucet

segments.t: About 43% of Midvale homes were built before 1980, so original pipes and older insulation are common. If your home is in that group, an hour of prep in October can prevent the most common winter calls.

blocks.text: Water Leak Alarms: A Cheap Early Warning

segments.t: Battery water-leak alarms cost little and sit on the floor near water heaters, washing machines, sinks and in basements. Many connect to your phone, so you get a warning while you're at work or traveling. Some systems can even shut off the main water valve automatically when a sensor gets wet. For homes with finished basements or rentals that sit empty between tenants, they're one of the simplest ways to catch a burst before it spreads.

blocks.text: Frozen Pipe FAQ
Should I leave faucets dripping every night in winter?

segments.t: Only during the coldest stretches, and only on faucets connected to pipes along outside walls or in cold spaces. A slow drip keeps water moving.

blocks.text: Can PEX pipes freeze?

segments.t: Yes. PEX flexes more than copper, but fittings and connections can still split when water inside freezes.

blocks.text: How do I find my main water shut-off?

segments.t: Look where the water line enters the house, usually in the basement or utility room near the water heater. In homes without basements, check a crawl space, garage or front closet.

blocks.text: What if a pipe bursts while I'm away?

segments.t: That's why keeping the heat on and having someone check the house matters. Water leak alarms near the water heater and in the basement can also alert you on your phone.

blocks.text: Is a frozen pipe an emergency if it hasn't burst?

segments.t: Treat it as one. Shut off the water to that line if you can, and thaw it carefully before it splits.

blocks.text: Pipe Burst in Your Midvale Home?

segments.t: If a pipe has already split and water is in your walls, ceilings or floors, call (385) 337-3560. A crew is dispatched immediately to remove the water and dry your home before the damage spreads.

pages.metaTitle: Swamp Cooler Winterizing Checklist for Midvale Homes | Utah Guide
pages.metaDescription: Step-by-step swamp cooler shutdown for Utah winters, plus the leak signs to catch early. Call (385) 337-3560 for ceiling leaks.
pages.h1: Swamp Cooler Winterizing Checklist for Midvale Homes
pages.intro: To winterize a swamp cooler in Midvale, shut off its water supply, drain the reservoir and water line, unplug the pump and motor, clean the pan, and cover the unit, ideally before the first hard freeze in early to mid-October. Skipping it can crack lines and pans and leak into your ceiling.

blocks.text: When should Midvale homeowners winterize a swamp cooler?

segments.t: Before the first hard freeze, usually by mid-October in the Salt Lake Valley: shut off the water line, drain the pan, and cover the cooler.

Swamp coolers are common on Midvale rooftops, especially on older ramblers and bungalows near Historic Main Street, Center Street and East Midvale, and on many 1960s to 1980s homes around Hillcrest and Midvale City Park. They work well in Utah's dry summers, but they run on a live water line. Once nights drop below freezing, any water left in the line, the float valve or the reservoir pan can freeze, expand and crack. The leak doesn't show up until the next warm afternoon, when the ice melts and water runs onto the roof or down the duct into the house.

blocks.text: Why Winterizing Matters

segments.t: A cooler that isn't winterized can cause problems all winter long:
Cracked water lines
leak onto the roof deck every time the ice melts.
Cracked reservoir pans
let water pool under the cooler.
Open ducts
let cold air into the house and warm, moist indoor air up into the duct, where it condenses and drips.
Snow and ice
collect inside an uncovered cooler and melt into the duct.
Damaged parts
mean repairs before you can run it next summer.
The result is often a stain around the ceiling vent, wet attic insulation and sometimes a sagging ceiling, discovered weeks after the damage started.

blocks.text: Step-by-Step Swamp Cooler Shutdown

segments.t: Work safely: only go on the roof if you're comfortable doing so, wear shoes with good grip, and don't work on a wet or icy roof. If you aren't sure, hire an HVAC company for this job.
Turn off the power.
Switch the cooler off at the thermostat or wall control, then unplug it or turn off its breaker.
Shut off the water supply.
Find the small valve on the water line that feeds the cooler. It's often in the attic, basement, utility room or on the line where it leaves the house. Turn it fully off.
Drain the water line.
Disconnect the line at the cooler or open the drain fitting so water left in the line runs out. A line that still holds water can freeze and split.
Drain the reservoir.
Open the drain plug or overflow in the bottom pan and let all the water out.
Clean the pan.
Scrub out scale, sediment and debris. Hard water leaves mineral buildup that makes float valves stick next season.
Check the float valve.
Look for scale or cracks so you can replace it before spring.
Check the pads.
Replace them now or note that they'll need replacing in spring.
Close the vent inside.
Close the ceiling vent or install an interior vent cover to keep warm air from rising into the duct.
Cover the cooler.
Use a fitted cooler cover to keep out snow, rain and wind.
Note the date.
Write down when you did it, for your own records.

blocks.text: Swamp Cooler Leak Signs to Catch Early

segments.t: Whether it's summer or winter, watch for these signs that water is getting where it shouldn't:
A brown or yellow ring around the ceiling vent.
Bubbling, peeling or cracked paint on the ceiling near the vent or along the duct path.
Water dripping from the vent grille.
A musty smell when the cooler runs, or when you open the vent.
Soft or sagging drywall in the room under the cooler.
Water running off the roof or down the gutter on a dry day.
Rust streaks on the outside of the cooler cabinet.
If you see any of these, turn the cooler off, shut its water valve, and check the attic if you can do so safely.

blocks.text: What Happens When You Skip It

segments.t: A common Midvale call goes like this: the cooler wasn't shut off before an early October freeze, the line cracked overnight, and the next sunny afternoon water started running across the roof deck and into the attic. Because the cooler wasn't running, nobody checked it. A week or two later, a stain shows up on the hallway ceiling. By then, blown-in insulation is soaked, the drywall is soft, and the roof sheathing may be growing mold.

At that point, the fix usually includes removing wet insulation, drying the attic and ceiling, treating any mold, and replacing ceiling drywall. Swamp Cooler Leak Water Damage (/swamp-cooler-leak-water-damage/)

blocks.text: Spring Start-Up Checklist

segments.t: When warm weather returns, usually in May:
Remove the cooler cover.
Clean the pan again and check for cracks.
Install new pads if needed.
Check and adjust the float valve so it shuts off well below the overflow.
Reconnect the water line and turn the supply valve back on slowly.
Watch the cooler fill and make sure the float stops the water.
Check the line and fittings for drips.
Open the ceiling vent and run the cooler while you watch for leaks.

blocks.text: A Midvale Swamp Cooler Calendar

rows: Start-up: cover off, clean, new pads, reconnect water, test the float
Check monthly for overflow, stains and musty smells
Shutdown: power off, water off, drain, clean, cover
Leave it covered; check the ceiling vent area for stains after storms

blocks.text: Hard Water and Your Cooler

segments.t: Midvale's water, like most water in the Salt Lake Valley, carries a lot of dissolved minerals. In a swamp cooler, the water evaporates and the minerals stay behind as scale on the pan, pads and float valve. Scale is the main reason float valves stick open and overflow. Cleaning the pan twice a year, replacing pads regularly and making sure the bleed-off line works all help keep scale under control.

blocks.text: Swamp Cooler or Central Air Condensate?

segments.t: If your home has central air instead of a swamp cooler, ceiling leaks can still happen from a clogged condensate line or drain pan at the indoor coil. Those leaks happen during summer use, not after freezing. If you have a ceiling stain and aren't sure which system caused it, the location usually tells you: under the cooler vent or its duct for a swamp cooler, near the furnace or attic air handler for central air. Ceiling Water Damage (/ceiling-water-damage/)

blocks.text: Side-Mount and Window Coolers

segments.t: Not every cooler sits on the roof. Side-mounted and window coolers need the same steps: shut off the water, drain the line and pan, unplug the unit and cover it. These coolers leak differently when they fail. Water runs down the outside wall, soaks the siding and sill, and can collect in a nearby window well or along the foundation. Inside, it shows up as a wet carpet edge or stained drywall below the window or wall opening. Seal the wall or window opening for winter so cold air and moisture stay out.

blocks.text: What a Cooler Leak Does to Your Attic

segments.t: Attics are where most swamp cooler damage hides. When water leaks onto the roof deck or runs down the duct:
Blown-in insulation
soaks up water, packs down and gets heavy enough to push on the ceiling drywall.
Roof sheathing and rafters
stay damp, which invites mold and rot.
Ceiling drywall
softens from above and can sag or come down.
The duct itself
can rust or collect standing water.

Wet insulation usually has to be removed, the attic dried and new insulation added once everything reads dry. That's why catching a leak early, or preventing it with a proper shutdown, saves so much trouble. Mold Remediation (/mold-remediation/)

blocks.text: Swamp Cooler Winterizing FAQ
Do I need to winterize a swamp cooler every year?

segments.t: Yes. Water left in the system will freeze during a Salt Lake Valley winter.

blocks.text: Can I leave water in the line if the valve is off?

segments.t: No. Water still in the line between the valve and the cooler can freeze and split it. Drain it.

blocks.text: Is a cooler cover really necessary?

segments.t: It keeps snow, rain and wind out of the cooler and duct, which cuts down on leaks and drafts all winter.

blocks.text: What if I already see a stain on my ceiling?

segments.t: Shut off the cooler's water and power, then have the ceiling and attic checked for wet insulation and mold.

blocks.text: Can I winterize a cooler myself?

segments.t: Many homeowners do, but roof work can be dangerous. If you're not comfortable on the roof, hire an HVAC company.

blocks.text: Stain Around Your Ceiling Vent?

segments.t: If your swamp cooler has already leaked into the attic or ceiling, call (385) 337-3560. A crew is dispatched immediately to dry the attic, remove wet insulation and repair the ceiling before the damage spreads.

pages.metaDescription: Who pays for unit-to-unit leaks in Utah condos, townhomes and apartments, and what to do first. Call (385) 337-3560.
pages.h1: Upstairs Unit Leaked Into Yours? Who Pays in a Utah Condo or Apartment
pages.intro: In most Utah condos and townhomes, who pays depends on where the leak started and what your HOA's governing documents say. The HOA master policy often covers shared structure, each owner's HO-6 covers their unit's interior, and renters need their own policy for belongings. Drying should start before anyone settles who pays.

blocks.text: Who pays when an upstairs neighbor's leak damages my Utah condo?

segments.t: It depends on where the leak began, your HOA's governing documents and each party's policy; the HOA master policy and owners' HO-6 policies often split the cost.

Unit-to-unit leaks are some of the most confusing water damage situations, because three or four parties can be involved at once: the owner of the unit where the leak started, the owner of the unit below, any renters living in either unit, and the HOA. Each has a different insurance policy covering a different part of the building. Utah's Condominium Ownership Act and your community's declaration (often called the CC&Rs) set the ground rules for who owns what and how the master policy deductible is handled. Because every community writes its documents a little differently, there's no single answer that fits every building. What is always true: the faster the water is removed and the better the damage is documented, the easier every part of the claim becomes.

blocks.text: What to Do First When Water Comes From Above

segments.t: Stop the water if you can.
Knock on the door of the unit above. If no one answers, call the property manager or HOA emergency line.
Protect yourself and your belongings.
Turn off power to the wet room if water is near lights or outlets, and move electronics and furniture out of the way.
Document everything.
Take photos and video of the ceiling, walls, floor and damaged belongings, with the date.
Notify the right people.
Tell the HOA or property manager, the upstairs owner or tenant, your landlord if you rent, and your own insurance company.
Start drying.
Don't wait for everyone to agree on who pays. Water keeps spreading and the damage grows each day. Condo & Apartment Water Damage (/condo-apartment-water-damage/)
Keep a written log
of who you spoke to, when, and what was said.

blocks.text: The Three Policies Involved
The HOA Master Policy

segments.t: The HOA's master policy covers the parts of the building the association is responsible for. Depending on the community, that may be just the exterior and common areas (sometimes called "bare walls"), or it may also include original interior finishes like drywall, cabinets and flooring. The master policy usually has a deductible, and many associations can pass part or all of that deductible to the owner whose unit caused the loss.

blocks.text: The Owner's HO-6 Policy

segments.t: An HO-6 is a condo owner's policy. It covers the parts of the unit the owner is responsible for under the HOA documents, along with personal belongings and liability. Two parts matter most for leaks:
Dwelling or "walls-in" coverage
for interior finishes the master policy doesn't cover.
Loss assessment coverage
, which can help pay an HOA deductible or special assessment charged to you.

blocks.text: The Renter's Policy

segments.t: Renters don't own the walls, floors or fixtures, so neither the HOA's policy nor the landlord's policy covers their belongings. A renters policy covers personal property, and often temporary housing costs if the unit can't be lived in. If you rent and don't have a policy, the cost of replacing your belongings usually falls to you.

blocks.text: A General Guide to Who Covers What

segments.t: Every community is different, so always check your governing documents and policies. This table shows how responsibility often splits.

rows: A pipe inside a shared wall or ceiling
The deductible may be charged to an owner in some cases

blocks.text: What If the Upstairs Neighbor Was Careless?

segments.t: If the leak came from something the upstairs owner or tenant did or failed to do, such as leaving a tub running or ignoring a dripping supply line, their liability coverage may come into play. In practice, your own insurer often pays your claim first and then seeks repayment from the other party's insurer. That process is called subrogation, and it's one reason to report the loss to your own insurer even when you're sure the other party is at fault.

blocks.text: Why Good Records Matter So Much

segments.t: In a single-family home, there's one owner and one policy. In a condo or apartment building, the same leak can touch several policies, and each adjuster wants to know exactly what was damaged in the part they cover. Clear records make that possible:
Separate photos for each unit
, labeled with the unit number.
Moisture readings
showing how far water traveled in each unit.
A list of removed materials
by unit and room.
Notes on the source
, including where the water started and when it was found.
Separate lists of tenant belongings
and owner-owned items.
That's the kind of documentation we keep on every multi-unit job, so the HOA, owners and renters each get what their insurer needs.

blocks.text: Common Unit-to-Unit Leak Sources in Midvale

segments.t: About a third of Midvale's housing units sit in buildings with 10 or more units, and many more are townhomes that share walls. In communities around Bingham Junction, Jordan Bluffs, View 72, the Fort Union corridor and Center Street, the most common sources are:
Washer hoses and drains in upstairs laundry closets.
Toilet supply lines and wax rings.
Dishwasher and fridge ice-maker lines.
Water heaters in upstairs utility closets.
Shower pans and tub drains.
Shared drain stack backups.
Fire sprinkler lines that freeze or get damaged.
For appliance-related leaks, see Water Heater & Appliance Leak Cleanup (/water-heater-leak-cleanup/).

blocks.text: Renters: Your Rights and Your Responsibilities

segments.t: In Utah, landlords are generally responsible for keeping rental units in a habitable condition, which includes fixing leaks and water damage to the structure. Renters are generally responsible for reporting problems promptly and for their own belongings. If a leak makes your unit unlivable, talk with your landlord about repairs and timing, and check whether your renters policy covers temporary housing. Keep copies of every message you send about the leak.

blocks.text: How to Protect Yourself Before It Happens

segments.t: Read your HOA documents
to see what the association covers and how deductibles are handled.
Check your HO-6 limits
for walls-in coverage and loss assessment coverage.
Get a renters policy
if you rent; it's usually inexpensive.
Replace rubber washer hoses
with braided stainless hoses.
Add water-leak alarms
near the washer, water heater and under sinks.
Shut off your washer valves
when you travel.
Report small drips and stains
to the HOA or manager right away.

blocks.text: What If the Leak Started in Your Unit?

segments.t: If the water came from your unit and damaged the one below, act fast and be upfront:
Shut off the water
at the fixture or your unit's main valve.
Tell your neighbor and the HOA or manager
right away.
Call your insurer
, since your HO-6 or renters liability coverage may be involved.
Get drying started
in both units, so the damage doesn't keep growing.
Keep your records
of the cause and the repair.
Quick action limits the damage you may be responsible for and keeps relationships with neighbors and the HOA on good terms.

blocks.text: Upstairs Leak FAQ
Should I call my own insurance company if the leak wasn't my fault?

segments.t: Usually yes. Your insurer can handle your claim and seek repayment from the responsible party's insurer.

blocks.text: Can drying start before the HOA decides who pays?

segments.t: Yes, and it should. Waiting only makes the damage and the claim larger for everyone.

blocks.text: My landlord says my belongings aren't their problem. Is that right?

segments.t: Usually, yes. A renters policy covers a tenant's belongings; the landlord's policy covers the building.

blocks.text: How long does it take to dry a condo after a leak from above?

segments.t: Most units dry in about 3 to 5 days. Ceilings, wall cavities and concrete floors can take longer.

pages.metaDescription: Utah air is dry, but wet walls are not. How fast mold grows after a leak and how to stop it. Call (385) 337-3560.
pages.eyebrow: MOLD AFTER A LEAK • MIDVALE, UTAH
pages.h1: Utah Is Too Dry for Mold? Why Wet Drywall Still Molds in Midvale
pages.intro: Yes, mold can grow in Utah. The outdoor air is dry, but the inside of a wet wall, a soaked carpet pad or a damp basement is not. Mold can start growing on wet drywall within about 24 to 48 hours, so how fast a leak is dried matters far more than the climate outside.

blocks.text: Can mold grow in Utah if the air is so dry?

segments.t: Yes. Outdoor air is dry, but a wet wall cavity or carpet pad holds moisture for days, which gives mold time to grow within 24 to 48 hours.

It's one of the most common things Midvale homeowners say after a leak: "It's Utah, it'll dry out on its own." The idea makes sense at first. Salt Lake Valley air is dry for much of the year, and a wet towel left outside dries quickly. But the inside of a wall isn't outside. Once water soaks into drywall, insulation, wood framing or carpet pad, it's trapped in a small, closed space where dry air can't reach it. That space stays damp for days or weeks, which is plenty of time for mold.

blocks.text: Outdoor Air vs Inside a Wet Wall

headers: Outdoor air in the Salt Lake Valley

segments.t: Mold spores are already in every home, floating in the air and settling on surfaces. They don't need much: moisture, something to eat, and a little time. A wet wall cavity gives them all three.

blocks.text: How Fast Mold Grows After a Leak

rows: Drywall, pad and wood soak up water; spores settle
Mold can begin growing on wet paper-faced drywall and dust
Growth may become visible in some areas; musty smells start
Growth spreads inside walls, under flooring and in attics
Materials can rot, odors set in and cleanup gets larger

segments.t: This is why the first two days after a leak decide how much of a home needs to be removed later.

blocks.text: Why Fans and Open Windows Aren't Enough

segments.t: Fans and open windows dry the surface you can see, but water inside walls, under flooring and in carpet pad stays put. A fan blowing across a wet wall can make the face of the drywall feel dry to the touch while the back stays soaked. In winter, opening windows lets in cold air that slows drying even more. And in Midvale's cold basements, concrete walls and floors stay cool, so moisture lingers longer than it would in a warm room.
Professional drying works differently:
Moisture meters and thermal imaging
find water you can't see.
Dehumidifiers
pull moisture out of the air so materials can release their water.
Air movers
push dry air across and into wet materials.
Wall-cavity drying
sends dry air inside walls through small holes behind baseboards.
Daily readings
show when materials match dry areas, so drying isn't stopped too early.

blocks.text: Where Mold Hides in Midvale Homes

segments.t: Finished basements:
paneling and drywall over cold concrete in Hillcrest and East Midvale ramblers and split-levels. Basement Flooding Cleanup (/basement-flooding-cleanup/)
Behind bathroom and kitchen walls:
slow leaks from supply lines, toilets and showers.
Attics:
under rooftop swamp coolers, around ice dams and above bathroom fans that vent into the attic.
Crawl spaces:
older homes near Historic Main Street with dirt floors and old pipes.
Under sinks and behind appliances:
dishwashers, fridges and water heaters.
Around windows:
window well leaks and winter condensation.

blocks.text: Signs Mold Has Already Started

segments.t: A musty or earthy smell that returns after cleaning.
Spots on drywall, baseboards, ceilings or wood, in black, green, gray or white.
Paint that bubbles, peels or stains.
Soft, warped or swollen drywall.
Allergy-like symptoms that ease when you leave the house.
If you notice any of these after a leak, the moisture needs to be found and fixed first, then the mold removed properly. Mold Remediation (/mold-remediation/)

blocks.text: Why Bleach and Paint Don't Fix It

segments.t: Bleach can lighten mold stains on hard surfaces like tile, but it doesn't reach growth inside drywall, wood or carpet, and the water in it can feed regrowth. Painting over mold just hides it while it keeps growing behind the paint. Lasting fixes do two things: remove the moldy material and fix the moisture that caused it.

blocks.text: Utah Has No State Mold License

segments.t: Utah doesn't license mold remediation companies at the state level. That makes the standard a company follows more important. The industry standard is IICRC S520. When you talk to anyone about mold, ask:
Do you follow the IICRC S520 standard?
Will you find and fix the moisture source first?
Will you set up containment and negative air?
What will be removed, and what will be cleaned?
Can independent testing be done afterward?

blocks.text: How to Prevent Mold After Any Leak

segments.t: Stop the water fast.
Know where your main shut-off is.
Start drying within 24 to 48 hours.
Don't wait to see if it dries on its own.
Measure, don't guess.
Use moisture readings to decide when things are dry.
Remove soaked pad and insulation
that can't be dried.
Keep basements below about 50% humidity
with a dehumidifier if they run damp.
Fix small drips quickly
under sinks, around toilets and at water heaters.
Vent bathroom fans outside
, not into the attic.
Winterize swamp coolers
before the first freeze.

blocks.text: The Cost of Waiting

segments.t: A leak dried within the first day or two often means extraction, drying and a few small repairs. The same leak left for a week or two can mean opening walls, removing insulation and drywall, containment for mold removal and a much bigger rebuild. General ranges in the Salt Lake area show the difference: drying a room after a leak often runs about $1,000 to $4,500, while mold remediation for small to mid-sized areas often runs about $1,500 to $6,000, before any rebuild. Acting early is the cheapest option by far. Emergency Water Extraction (/emergency-water-extraction/)

rows: Cool concrete, groundwater, water heaters nearby
Musty smell, stains at the bottom of walls, damp carpet edges
Daily steam, shower and toilet leaks
Spots on ceilings and grout, soft floors near the toilet

blocks.text: A Quick Musty-Smell Checklist

segments.t: If a room smells musty, check these spots before anything else:
Under the kitchen and bathroom sinks.
Behind and under the dishwasher and fridge.
Around the base of toilets.
Under the washer and around the water heater.
Along the bottom of basement walls and under carpet edges.
Around windows and window wells.
Around the ceiling vent if you have a swamp cooler.
If you find dampness or spots, stop using the leaking fixture if you can and have the area checked with a moisture meter. Water Leak Detection (/water-leak-detection/)

blocks.text: Utah Mold FAQ
Is black mold more dangerous than other mold?

segments.t: Color doesn't tell you the type, and any mold can cause problems for sensitive people. Large or hidden growth should be removed properly, whatever its color.

blocks.text: Can I just run a dehumidifier after a leak?

segments.t: A dehumidifier helps, but water trapped in walls, pad and subfloors needs air movement and sometimes opening up to dry in time.

blocks.text: Will mold die once the area dries?

segments.t: It stops growing, but dead mold can still cause odors and irritation, so it should still be removed.

blocks.text: How do I know if my walls are dry?

segments.t: Moisture readings in the wet area should match readings in a dry area of the same home.

blocks.text: Does homeowners insurance cover mold?

segments.t: Mold from a sudden, covered water event may be covered, often up to a limit. Mold from long-term leaks or humidity usually isn't.

blocks.text: Had a Leak in Your Midvale Home?

segments.t: Don't count on Utah's dry air to finish the job. Call (385) 337-3560 and a crew is dispatched immediately to dry your home properly, or to remove mold if it's already started.

pages.metaTitle: Water Coming Up Through Your Basement Floor? Spring Snowmelt in Midvale
pages.metaDescription: Why Midvale basements seep in spring, what to do the first hour, and when to call for help. Call (385) 337-3560.
pages.h1: Water Coming Up Through Your Basement Floor? Spring Snowmelt in Midvale
pages.intro: Water coming up through a basement floor in spring, with no broken pipe, is usually groundwater. As Wasatch snowmelt soaks the valley's clay soil, pressure builds under and around the foundation and pushes water through floor cracks, wall joints and window wells, even on dry, sunny days.

blocks.text: Why does my Midvale basement flood in spring without rain?

segments.t: Melting mountain snow saturates the valley's clay soil and lifts groundwater, which pushes up through floor cracks and window wells even on dry, sunny days.

Every spring, the snowpack in the Wasatch melts and runs down into the Salt Lake Valley through creeks, canals and the ground itself. Midvale sits on the valley floor, between the mountains to the east and the Jordan River on its west edge, on fine, clay-rich soil. Clay holds water and swells. When the ground around your foundation is full, water looks for the easiest way into the low point of the house, which is the basement. That's why a basement can take on water on a warm, sunny afternoon in April or May, days after the last storm.

blocks.text: How to Tell Groundwater From a Leak

rows: Along the floor-wall joint, through slab cracks, across a wide area
Near one fixture, pipe or appliance
Spring runoff, after long watering, weeks after storms
Can be fast and from one direction
Clean from supply lines, or gray from drains

segments.t: If the meter moves with everything off, look for a plumbing leak first. If it doesn't, and water is coming from the floor or wall joints, groundwater is the likely cause.

blocks.text: Where Snowmelt Gets Into Midvale Basements

segments.t: The floor-wall joint:
the seam where the slab meets the foundation wall is the most common entry point.
Slab cracks:
hairline and settlement cracks let water rise under pressure.
Wall cracks and tie holes:
small openings in poured concrete or block walls.
Pipe penetrations:
where water, sewer or gas lines pass through the wall.
Window wells:
meltwater and runoff fill the well and pour in around the window. Window Well Flooding (/window-well-flooding/)
Floor drains:
in some cases, saturated ground pushes water up through the floor drain.

blocks.text: What to Do in the First Hour

segments.t: Move furniture, boxes, electronics and rugs off the floor.
Turn off power to the basement if water is near outlets and the panel is safe to reach.
Check the water meter with everything off to rule out a plumbing leak.
Look outside: point downspouts away from the house, turn off sprinklers, and lower water in window wells from outside if safe.
Take photos and video of where the water is coming in.
Pull back wet area rugs; leave wall-to-wall carpet in place until a crew can lift it properly.
Call (385) 337-3560 so water removal and drying can start.

blocks.text: Why Seepage Needs More Than a Shop Vac

segments.t: Groundwater seepage is usually wide and shallow. It soaks carpet pad across large areas, wicks up the bottom of drywall and paneling, and gets under laminate and vinyl plank. A shop vac picks up the surface water, but the pad, the bottom of the walls and the floor underneath stay wet. In Midvale's cool basements, that moisture can sit for weeks, which leads to musty smells and mold. Proper drying includes extraction from the pad, moisture mapping of walls and floors, dehumidifiers and air movers, and daily readings until everything matches dry areas. Basement Flooding Cleanup (/basement-flooding-cleanup/)

blocks.text: Which Midvale Basements Seep Most

segments.t: Lower ground on the west side
, closer to the Jordan River, where the water table sits higher in wet springs.
Older homes near Historic Main Street and Center Street
, with older foundations, partial basements and crawl spaces.
Finished basements in Hillcrest and East Midvale ramblers and split-levels
, where paneling and carpet over concrete hide seepage.
Homes where yards slope toward the house
, or where soil has settled next to the foundation.
Homes with downspouts that empty right beside the walls.

blocks.text: Fixes That Reduce Spring Seepage

segments.t: These are usually done after the basement is dry, by a landscaper, handyman or waterproofing contractor:

rows: Extend downspouts several feet from the house
Keeps roof water away from the foundation
Regrade soil to slope away from the walls
Sends surface water away instead of toward the house
Clear or upgrade window well drains and add covers
Stops wells from filling and spilling inside
Interior drain system and sump pump
Collects groundwater under the slab and pumps it out

segments.t: The first three are inexpensive and often make the biggest difference. A sump system is the bigger fix for basements that seep every year.

blocks.text: Sandbags and Spring Prep

segments.t: In heavy runoff years, Salt Lake County and local cities often make sandbags available. Locations change from year to year, so check county and city announcements when high runoff is forecast. Sandbags are most useful at window wells, garage doors and outside basement stairs. They're less useful against groundwater, which comes up from below. Midvale Water & Sewer Emergency Contacts (/midvale-water-sewer-emergency-contacts/)

blocks.text: Does Insurance Cover Spring Seepage?

segments.t: This is the hard part. Most homeowners policies exclude damage from groundwater, surface water and seepage. Flood insurance covers some surface flooding but often has limits on basement contents and finishes. A sudden plumbing failure is usually covered, which is one reason to rule out a leak first. Policies vary, so check yours and talk to your agent before spring.

blocks.text: A Spring Checklist for Midvale Basements

segments.t: A little prep in late winter can keep spring runoff outside where it belongs.
February to March:
Clear leaves and debris from gutters, downspouts and window well gravel.
Make sure every downspout empties several feet from the foundation.
Install or check window well covers.
Test your sump pump, if you have one, by pouring water into the pit.
Move keepsakes, papers and electronics off basement floors and into plastic bins on shelves.
April to June (peak runoff):
Walk the basement every few days, especially along outside walls and corners.
Lift a corner of carpet near the walls to check for dampness underneath.
Watch window wells after warm afternoons and storms.
Hold off on heavy watering right next to the foundation.

blocks.text: Seepage and Mold: Why the Clock Matters

segments.t: Seepage water is often clean, but it soaks into carpet pad, the bottom of drywall and paneling, and any cardboard boxes on the floor. Basements stay cool and dark, which slows drying and gives mold a chance to start within a couple of days. A musty smell weeks after the water seemed to stop usually means moisture is still trapped under flooring or inside the walls. Drying it properly the first time is the best way to avoid a mold problem later. Mold Remediation (/mold-remediation/)

blocks.text: What It Generally Costs

segments.t: General ranges for planning in the Salt Lake area:
Small area of seepage caught early: about $1,500 to $3,500
Finished basement with wet carpet, pad and walls: about $2,500 to $9,000
Cost depends on how much area is wet, how long it sat, the flooring and wall finishes, and how many days of drying are needed. Waterproofing work outside is separate.

blocks.text: Spring Snowmelt FAQ
When is spring runoff season in Midvale?

segments.t: Usually from about March through June, peaking when warm weather melts high-elevation snow quickly.

blocks.text: Will the water stop on its own?

segments.t: Usually, once runoff slows and the soil drains. But the water already inside needs to be removed and dried to prevent mold.

blocks.text: Can I seal the floor from inside to stop it?

segments.t: Sealing cracks helps with small seepage, but strong groundwater pressure often finds another way in. Drainage outside and a sump system work better for serious seepage.

blocks.text: Should I pull up my carpet?

segments.t: Leave wall-to-wall carpet down until a crew can lift and dry it properly; pulling it yourself can tear the backing and make it harder to save.

blocks.text: Why does it happen every year?

segments.t: The soil and drainage around your home haven't changed. Fixing grading, downspouts and window wells, or adding a sump system, breaks the cycle.
